## The sketch

The whole sketch is three lines — the `UsbIo` library does the rest:

```cpp
#include <UsbIo.h>
void setup() { UsbIo.begin(); }
void loop()  { UsbIo.poll(); }
```

`UsbIo.begin()` brings up the vendor USB interface; `UsbIo.poll()`, called
every `loop()` iteration, drains queued commands from the host and refreshes
the pin-state shadow that reads answer from. Nothing else needs to be in the
sketch for the board to work as an AMLab bench — see [Adding your own
code](#adding-your-own-code) if you want to add something.


::: {.callout-tip title="Dual core on Portenta H7"}

The Portenta H7 has two asymmetrical cores: a fast one and a slower one (roughly
half clock). Since v0.4.1 of the UsbIo library there is a second sketch,
`UsbDeviceLED`, only suitable for Portenta boards, that runs the main UsbIo
firmware on the main core, and a simple LED blinking firmware on the second
core. The latter allows to easily customize the blink pattern and make it easier
to spot a board that has the UsbIo firmware running. Since the blinking formware
runs on a separate core, it won't affect in any way the performance of the UsbIo
firmware, which is running on the main core.

Also see
[the ArduinoDriver examples folder](https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver/tree/main/examples).

:::


## Install the core, once per machine

Install the Arduino core for your board before the first upload. With
`arduino-cli` (see [Supported boards](boards.qmd#tbl-boards-detail) for every
core name):

```bash
arduino-cli core install arduino:mbed_portenta   # Portenta H7
arduino-cli core install arduino:mbed_giga       # GIGA R1 WiFi
arduino-cli core install arduino:mbed_nano       # Nano 33 BLE, Nano RP2040 Connect
arduino-cli core install arduino:renesas_uno     # UNO R4 Minima, Nano R4
arduino-cli core install arduino:samd            # Zero, MKR family, Nano 33 IoT
```

In the Arduino IDE, the same cores install from *Tools ▸ Board ▸ Boards
Manager*.

## Three ways to flash

### Arduino IDE

Install *UsbIo* from the Library Manager (*Tools ▸ Manage Libraries*, search
"UsbIo"), or clone/symlink the ArduinoDriver repository into your sketchbook's
`libraries/` folder. Then open *File ▸ Examples ▸ UsbIo ▸ UsbIoDevice*, select
your board and port, and press Upload.

If you have a dual core portenta, pick *File ▸ Examples ▸ UsbIo ▸ UsbIoDeviceLED*, then program your board twice: first after selecting *Tools ▸ Target core: "Main Core"*, then after selecting *Tools ▸ Target core: "M4 Co-processor"*. This will give you the blinking blue LED.

### `arduino-cli`, from a clone

Find the port, then compile and upload in one step. `--library .` makes the
repository itself the library, so nothing needs to be installed separately:

```bash
arduino-cli board list          # -> /dev/cu.usbmodem1102, arduino:mbed_portenta:envie_m7
arduino-cli compile --fqbn arduino:mbed_portenta:envie_m7 --library . \
  --warnings all -u -p /dev/cu.usbmodem1102 examples/UsbIoDevice
```

Drop `-u -p <port>` to compile without uploading.

### CMake targets

When `arduino-cli` is on `PATH`, the root `CMakeLists.txt` adds one target per
board: `firmware-portenta`, `firmware-giga`, `firmware-nano33ble`,
`firmware-nanorp2040`, `firmware-minima`, `firmware-nanor4`,
`firmware-mkrzero`, `firmware-nano33iot`, `firmware-zero`, plus
`firmware-all` for every core you have installed:

```bash
cmake -Bbuild -G Ninja
cmake --build build --target firmware-portenta      # -> build/firmware/portenta
```

Uploading needs the port in the CMake cache, so it is a two-step affair:

```bash
cmake -Bbuild -DUSBIO_UPLOAD_PORT=/dev/cu.usbmodem1102
cmake --build build --target upload-portenta
```

## Bootloader and the changing port

::: {.callout-warning}
## The port changes twice

**If the upload fails to find the board**, put it in bootloader mode:
double-tap the reset button on mbed boards (Portenta, GIGA, Nano 33 BLE) —
the LED breathes — and on SAMD boards too. The board enumerates under a
*different* port in bootloader mode, so re-run `arduino-cli board list` and
use the new port.

The port changes **again** after a successful upload, when the board
re-enumerates running `UsbIo`. Re-run `arduino-cli board list` (or `arduino-io
list` once the host driver is built) if you need the port a second time.
:::

## Check it worked

This needs the host driver from [setting up a bench, step
3](index.qmd#setup-order):

```bash
arduino-io info
```

should report the board's name, pin counts and resolutions, and its `flags`
line tells you which firmware capabilities are present. See [Verifying a
bench](verify.qmd) for the full procedure and the expected output.

## Adding your own code {#adding-your-own-code}

The sketch can do other things too, as long as it follows a few rules:

```cpp
#include <UsbIo.h>

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
  UsbIo.begin();
}

void loop() {
  UsbIo.poll(); // runs the commands from the computer: call it on every loop

  // Your own code: keep it short, and never call delay().
  static unsigned long last = 0;
  if (millis() - last >= 500) {
    last = millis();
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, !digitalRead(LED_BUILTIN)); // heartbeat
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Why these rules matter for AMLab

- **Keep `loop()` fast.** Commands from the host wait until the next
  `UsbIo.poll()`, and **streaming takes at most one sample per `poll()`** —
  the sketch's loop rate is the hard ceiling on the achieved sampling rate
  for every streaming experiment (S1–S3, M3). Slow code in your own part of
  `loop()` lowers that ceiling for everyone using the board.
- **Never call `delay()`.** It blocks `poll()` for its whole duration, which
  both stalls host commands and, during a stream, shows up as a longer gap
  in `t_us` rather than a burst of catch-up samples.
- **Don't drive a pin from both sides.** `UsbIo` leaves every pin alone until
  the host sets its mode, so your own `Serial1`, SPI or LED code keeps
  working undisturbed — but do not have the sketch and the host both write
  the same pin.
- **A host reset puts every pin back to `INPUT`.** `arduino-io reset` (or
  `reset()`/`dev$reset()` in the bindings) reconfigures *every* pin the host
  can address, including ones your own code was using. If your sketch relies
  on a pin staying in a particular mode, re-apply that mode after a reset, or
  keep the host driver from resetting it.
- **`Serial` stays yours.** The CDC serial port is untouched by `UsbIo`, so
  `Serial.print()` remains available for your own debugging throughout.
:::


::: callout-tip
### Remote procedure call

The `UsbIo` library also exposes a remote procedure call mechanism: you can add
your own function in the sketch and call it from the host. See the
[ArduioDriver documentation](https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver).

:::
